power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Compulsive rituals in OCD present a fundamental puzzle for theories of human learning.
How can an action acquire value as a means of preventing harm even though the individual recognizes that the action has little or no causal influence on the feared outcome?

We propose that this apparent contradiction can arise from automatic credit assignment, whereby actions that precede favorable outcomes are reinforced even when those actions are known to be causally irrelevant.
When harm is anticipated but no adverse outcome occurs, the absence of harm may reinforce the preceding action, allowing an objectively ineffective behavior to acquire harm prevention value.
We formalize this account using an actor-critic reinforcement learning model in which actions are performed under fluctuating states of subjective perceived threat.
Simulations show that agents possessing such false credit assignment mechanisms develop persistent ritualistic behavior in an objectively uncontrollable environment.
We find that ritualistic behavior is especially likely to persist when feared outcomes are rare and highly aversive, making the ritual appear consistently effective in preventing a catastrophe.

We further describe the cost-effectiveness of ritualistic behavior, 1 and provide a computational account of how compulsive rituals can emerge as goal-directed attempts to prevent harm, persist despite explicit causal knowledge, and subsequently acquire anxiety-reducing properties.
This work may help explain the persistence of compulsive behavior and inform mechanisms through which therapy can reduce it.

text.text: Consequently, identifying the computational cognitive processes that facilitate these behaviors is a crucial objective for understanding human behavior.

Here, we build on recent findings about automatic aspects of human value learning to develop a mechanistic framework for how compulsive behavior can be developed and maintained in the absence of a causal link between actions and the catastrophe they are aimed to prevent.
Our framework is based on the idea that compulsive rituals are often reinforced by the nonoccurrence of a catastrophe that had been unjustifiably anticipated (Salkovskis, 1998).

text.text: We propose that this natural account can arise from the interaction of two mechanisms.
First, action values are updated automatically based on action-outcome contiguity, even when this association conflicts with explicit knowledge.
Second, the anticipated catastrophic event is rare and therefore usually does not occur following the execution of the ritual.
The suggestion that illusory action-outcome associations can lead to ritualistic behavior was first introduced by animal studies.

Classic experiments showed that pigeons developed repetitive and idiosyncratic behaviors such as pecking or jumping when food was delivered at fixed intervals regardless of their actions, leading Skinner (Skinner, 1948) to describe these behaviors as a form of superstition (Reberg et al., 1978; Staddon & Simmelhag, 1971; Timberlake & Lucas, 1985).

text.text: A second central feature of our proposed mechanism is that, because catastrophic events are rare, ritualistic actions will usually be followed by the absence of disaster.

In the reinforcement learning literature, the discrepancy between an expected outcome and an experienced outcome is commonly referred to as a prediction error and is considered a primary driver of learning (Bayer & Glimcher, 2005; Schultz et al., 1997).

text.text: Thus, the positive prediction error typically experienced after performing the ritualistic action may reinforce it.
In this way, ritualistic actions performed under a state of internal threat may be assigned undue credit for the nonoccurrence of disaster, causing them to be experienced as having "neutralized" it.
Over time, this repeated reinforcement strengthens the behavior, making the compulsive ritual increasingly resistant to extinction.

Our proposed mechanism is intended to complement existing accounts of compulsive rituals by addressing an important question concerning how a causally irrelevant action comes to acquire value as a harm-preventive response in the first place.
Prominent theoretical accounts have emphasized mechanisms such as anxiety reduction and habit formation.
However, as we review below, each captures only part of the phenomenon and leaves some aspects of ritual emergence unexplained.

Perhaps the most influential mechanistic account of the persistence of compulsive ritualistic behavior proposes that rituals are negatively reinforced by the reduction in anxiety or distress that follows their performance (Hezel & Simpson, 2019).

text.text: We thereby offer a complementary account of the processes that may contribute to the onset and maintenance of human compulsive rituals.
To illustrate our proposed mechanism, we use an artificial reinforcement learning agent that models compulsive rituals in human behavior.
Throughout the paper, we specify the mental and environmental conditions under which individuals may come to develop rituals that are causally unrelated to harm prevention.
We then illustrate how these can be mechanistically connected with stress reduction.

We propose that the onset and maintenance of ritualistic behavior can arise from the combination of specific environmental conditions, such as rare negative events and low-cost actions, with automatic action-outcome value learning.

This combination can lead an agent to develop ritualistic behavior that is reinforced as if it prevents a perceived catastrophe, despite the absence of any causal relationship in the external environment.
To explore and describe how the two components above could lead to the formation and maintenance of compulsive rituals, we implement them in reinforcement learning agent model simulations.
We manipulate external (environmental) and internal (within-agent) factors, allowing us to explore the conditions under which actions might be falsely learned as causally linked to harm prevention.
We start by providing a general outlook of the mechanistic components that are included in the simulations and follow with a mathematical description of the model.
One question that arises is how to define compulsive behavior in an artificial agent.

Here, we follow the DSM-5 definition and assess compulsive ritual-like behavior as the repeated selection of an action that the agent associates with harm prevention, even though no such association exists in the simulated environment.
In computational modeling, the 'environment' refers to the external world and the rules that govern it.
Although these rules are not fully observable in real life, in our simulation, they can be artificially manipulated to reveal the conditions under which compulsive rituals may emerge.
In line with our theoretical conditions, we start by simulating a reinforcement learning agent operating in an environment where catastrophes rarely occur.
Critically, the occurrence of a catastrophic event is unrelated by design to the agent's actions.
The "agent" reflects the internal psychological processes governing behavior.
While the agent is not aware of the environment's rules, it tries to adapt its behavior based on perceived events.
We simulate "psychological triggers" that induce in the agent the false belief that a catastrophe is highly likely to occur.
Based on its current belief about the likelihood of a catastrophe, the agent transitions between two internal mental states, each associated with a distinct action policy.
When the agent believes that a catastrophe is highly likely to occur, it enters the "Anxious" mental state, whereas when it believes that a catastrophe is unlikely, it enters the "Calm" mental state.
When acting in the "Anxious" state, where a catastrophe is anticipated, the agent may misattribute the absence of catastrophe to their own behavior, thereby reinforcing arbitrary actions.

This mechanism depends on the degree to which the agent tends to automatically assign credit to its actions, making agents with a stronger tendency toward such learning especially prone to developing ritual-like behaviors.

text.text: Reward function.

In the simulated environments, regardless of the actions performed, the agent experiences a catastrophic negative reward (here, v harm =-100) with probability freq(c), and a neutral zero reward otherwise.
We start by describing an environment in which catastrophic events never occur [i.e., freq(c) = 0].

We modeled the agent's internal threat belief at time t as p(harm) t , representing the subjective belief that the catastrophe will occur, regardless of its true probability in the environment (i.e., freq(c)).
To generate this belief, we used a cyclic triggering event that recurred every 100 time steps.
We initialized the harm estimate (i.e., h) to 0 and updated it at each time step based on whether a triggering event occurred.
The harm estimate decayed on each time step toward 0 according to a relaxation rate bounded between 0 and 1, reflecting the tendency for stress to subside naturally over time.
See Eq. 10 below for a description of how the relaxation rate changed in each timestep t.
We then defined p(harm), the agent's perceived probability that a catastrophe would occur, as a scaled inverse logit transformation of h.
This transformation mapped the accumulated harm signal onto a probability while accounting for the strictly positive nature of h.

Specifically, the expected value in a given time step, t, is the multiplication of the belief regarding the probability of harm with the belief regarding its negative valence.

Simulation 1 demonstrates how a reinforcement learning agent might acquire ritualistic-like behavior.
Specifically, we estimated the frequency of the RL agent repeating a particular action when harm was highly expected.
In our model, this behavior emerges through three interacting mechanisms.
First, action values (i.e., propensities) are updated according to an advantage estimate, A t (Eq. 8), defined as the difference between the observed reward and the current state value.
Specifically, when the agent's internal state value is negative (reflecting the belief that harm is highly probable), the estimated state value becomes negative.
Because all outcomes in this simulation are neutral (no harm is ever observed), the agent experiences a positive advantage, A t .
For the agent with high automatic credit assignment, this positive advantage increases the value of the recently selected action, as though that action had caused safety (Eq.
In this way, the absence of harm functions as positive reinforcement under elevated threat, consistent with cognitive accounts of compulsive behavior (Salkovskis, 1985).

text.text: Thus, the simulation shows how, in an anxious state, an agent can quickly learn to repeat the action that happened to precede a neutral outcome, despite no causal control.
Second, low values of η, reflecting the agent's ability to refrain from assigning undue credit, protect against the acquisition of these nonveridical action values.
This finding highlights how automatic credit assignment can lead to the emergence of ritualistic-like behavior in a noncontrollable environment.
Third, the model links confidence in action selection to an increased rate of relaxation.
As a result, once a ritualized response is acquired, performing it accelerates the reduction of perceived threat.
Simulation 1 demonstrated that an agent can acquire ritualistic-like behavior following a gap between a negative expectation and a neutral outcome.
A significant question that follows is to what extent the features of the feared event can influence the acquisition of ritualistic behaviors.

In the clinical realm, compulsive ritualistic human behavior is usually characterized as an action driven by an intense fear of a catastrophic event (i.e., death, serious illness, etc.; Abramowitz & Jacoby, 2014).

text.text: However, catastrophic events are typically very rare.
We propose that this rarity supports the maintenance of ritualistic behavior.

If the feared catastrophe occurred frequently, then, according to our theoretical framework, the ritualistic action would be expected to extinguish, because negative value would be assigned to the action that preceded the catastrophe.

In the current experiment, we therefore examine whether the reinforcement learning mechanism described in Simulation 1 promotes a higher incidence of ritual-like behavior, particularly when the feared event is rare in the external environment, and its internal valence is catastrophic (i.e., very negative valence).
To this end, we used the same actor-critic model as before (Eqs. 1 to 10) and generated three groups of agents with 100 agents in each group (total N=300).

The first group was simulated with parameters similar to those of the high automatic credit assignment agent in Simulation 1, with a minimal probability for the occurrence of a catastrophe (see Methods).
This allowed us to re-examine the frequency of ritualistic-like behaviors across multiple agents, while also serving as a baseline comparison (i.e., baseline group).

The second group of agents was a high catastrophe frequency group, where the frequency with which the harmful event occurred in the environment (i.e., freq(c)) was higher compared with the baseline group.
The third group of agents was a low catastrophe valence group, where we reduced the extent to which the predicted negative outcome was experienced as catastrophic (i.e., v harm ).

The baseline group was assigned parameters reflecting high automatic credit assignment, low frequency of the negative event and a high negative valence for that event (500 timesteps with a trigger every 100 time steps and a trigger intensity of 5 points; relax rate of 0.95, threshold calm to anxious state transition = 0.05; automatic credit assignment of η=0.1; frequency of catastrophic outcome of freq(c) ~ Beta(1,1000); valence of catastrophic event of v harm ~ N(-100, 5); see Eq 1 to 10).

text.text: In Simulation 2, we described two manipulations that can alter the agent's tendency toward repetitive behavior when in the anxious state.
First, we increased the frequency of catastrophic outcomes in the environment.
In our model, repetitive behavior is sustained because a neutral and safe outcome tends to follow the execution of the repeated action.

Increasing the frequency of catastrophes disrupts this mechanism and prevents the maintenance of the ritual, because the repeated action is then more often followed by the very outcome it is meant to prevent.
This highlights a central implication of the model, namely that an objectively safe environment is an important condition for the emergence of rituals.
Second, reducing the subjective valence assigned to the harmful event weakened the development of ritualistic behavior.
When the feared negative event is represented as less severe, the omission of a negative outcome following action execution provides weaker reinforcement.
This suggests that when an actor is able to appraise the anticipated harm as relatively small, repetitive ritual-like behavior tendencies may diminish.

In previous experiments, we proposed a computational mechanism for the emergence and maintenance of ritualistic-like behavior, whereby agents with elevated anticipated harm falsely attributed the non-occurrence of feared outcomes to their own actions.
These simulations showed that such behavior is strengthened when the environment is objectively safe, and the anticipated negative outcome is subjectively severe.
Yet, a central assumption in these experiments was that all actions were identical in their propensity to be acquired as rituals.
However, from a clinical perspective, it is clear that some actions are more prone to becoming ritualistic (Pinciotti et al., 2023).

text.text: In Simulation 3, we therefore examine the factors that make certain actions more likely to become ritualized.

Compulsive rituals often build on relatively simple actions, such as washing, checking, ordering, repeating, or counting, whose clinical cost only emerges as they become excessive, repetitive, and time-consuming (Pinciotti et al., 2023).

text.text: For example, hand washing is initially a simple and low-cost action, but when repeated excessively, it can consume substantial time, impair functioning, or cause physical harm.
We therefore examine how the cost associated with different actions influences which action is more likely to become ritualized.
A second factor that may distinguish actions that become ritualistic from those that do not is the level of associability of each action.
Clinically, compulsions are often contextually linked to the feared outcome.
For example, contamination-related obsessions are commonly accompanied by washing rituals, because washing is perceived as capable of reducing contamination-related harm.
More generally, when a feared catastrophe does not occur, the resulting relief may be more readily attributed to actions that are contextually associated with the negative outcome.
To capture these aspects, we manipulate the associability parameter, β a , which reflects the degree to which a given action can be associated with harm prevention.
We simulated a group of 200 agents while varying the repetition cost parameter of each action (pr a ) across agents.
Specifically, the repetition cost for each action was sampled from a wide distribution, pr a ~|N(0.5,0.5)|, and all actions had a fixed cost decay, f p =0.01.
All other parameters were identical to those of the high automatic credit assignment agent in Simulation 1.
We estimated the association between the action's cost and its probability of becoming ritualistic.

In a second sample, we simulated a group of 200 agents and varied the associability parameter, which captures, for each action, the degree to which the agent would potentially associate it with harm prevention.
Specifically, the associability parameters were sampled from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1 (i.e.,β a ~Beta(1,1)).
We show that actions with a lower repetition cost are more readily acquired as rituals.
Specifically, we find a negative association between the action's cost and the probability with which it is acquired as a ritual (posterior median = -0.24, HDI 95% [-0.31, -0.18]).

We further illustrate that actions that are a priori seen as contextually associated with the occurrence of an anticipated harm are more likely to become ritualistic, as indicated by a positive association between the action's associability parameter and the probability with which it is acquired as ritualistic (posterior median = 0.30, HDI 95% [0.22, 0.37]). rituals.
Not all actions are equally likely to be acquired as rituals.
For example, hand washing is a more common ritual compared to jumping.
To illustrate that, in Simulation 3, we separated the ten actions based on two action-specific parameters: repetition cost (pr a ) and associability (β a ).
The repetition cost parameter (pr a ) reflects the cost accumulated for each time a given action is done.
For example, the cost of a single instance of hand washing is expected to be lower than the cost of a single instance of jumping.
Second, we introduced an associability parameter that captures for each action how likely it is to be assigned credit for harm prevention.
This captures the idea that, in the context of contamination fear, for example, hand washing is more readily associated with harm prevention than an action such as jumping.
In this experiment, we demonstrate how different action properties can affect ritualistic-like behavior.

First, we introduce the notion of a repetition cost that accumulates as the agent excessively repeats an action, highlighting that ritualistic behavior often involves relatively low-cost actions that become debilitating only following their excessive repetition.
Second, we differentiate between actions in terms of how likely they are to be assigned credit for the nonoccurrence of an anticipated catastrophe.

For example, a "washing" ritual compared to a "jumping" ritual is more likely to develop in reaction to a contamination fear, as washing is both comparatively less costly and more typically associated with preventing contamination.
This work provides a theoretical computational account of how compulsive ritualistic behavior may be acquired and maintained despite having no causal influence on a feared outcome.
For this purpose, we modeled an actor-critic reinforcement learning agent operating in an environment in which catastrophic outcomes were rare and causally unrelated to the agent's actions.

This illustrates the main mechanism suggested by the model, showing how the absence of an anticipated threat can reinforce causally unrelated actions.
Having established in Simulation 1 how a ritualistic-like behavior can emerge in our model, Simulation 2 addressed the question of what factors support its maintenance.
Interestingly, ritualistic-like behavior was more likely to be maintained when the feared event was objectively very rare and subjectively highly aversive.
Specifically, increasing the frequency of the negative event or reducing its subjective negative valence decreased ritualistic-like behavior.
A main driving force of compulsive behavior, according to our model, is that from the agent's perspective, the ritual always works.
As the feared catastrophe becomes more common, the ritual is increasingly followed by the very outcome the agent seeks to prevent, causing its acquired value to extinguish over time.

Thus, somewhat counterintuitively, a largely safe environment, coupled with the expectation of a highly aversive outcome, may provide particularly favorable conditions for the maintenance of ritualistic behavior (Gillan & Robbins, 2014).

text.text: Inhibitory learning accounts of exposure propose that exposure establishes new learning rather than eliminating the original threat association, leaving previously learned responses susceptible to later recovery under certain conditions (Craske et al., 2008 (Craske et al., , 2014)).

text.text: Thus, following the termination of ERP treatment, when the therapist no longer imposes an "external cost" on performing the ritual, the previously learned ritual response may compete with newly acquired learning, particularly when threat is encountered again outside the treatment context.
An important implication of such response prevention treatment concerns the possibility of ritual substitution.

Because the mechanism proposed here can, in principle, assign harm-prevention value to alternative actions performed under threat, preventing one specific ritual may leave open the possibility that another overt or covert response would be reinforced instead.

If the anticipated threat remains high and alternative rituals are not restricted by the therapist, the same learning mechanism may allow these alternative actions to acquire harm-prevention value and become ritualized.

This possibility is consistent with clinical accounts emphasizing that avoidance, reassurance, and mental compulsions may interfere with ERP, and in some cases, replace the overt ritual prevented during treatment (Gillihan et al., 2012).
text.formatted: This possibility is consistent with clinical accounts emphasizing that avoidance, reassurance, and mental compulsions may interfere with ERP, and in some cases, replace the overt ritual prevented during treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Gillihan et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, effective response prevention may require addressing not only the primary ritual, but also attending to other responses that may receive credit for the nonoccurrence of the feared outcome during treatment.

Notably, our simulations were limited to actions performed in the context of an anticipated negative outcome, whereas superstitious behaviors may also arise when seeking to promote desirable outcomes, for example in sports or gambling (Dömötör et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Notably, our simulations were limited to actions performed in the context of an anticipated negative outcome, whereas superstitious behaviors may also arise when seeking to promote desirable outcomes, for example in sports or gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Dömötör et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: First, the distinction between these two types of motivations may be less clear-cut in practice.
Many situations in which positive-outcome rituals occur can be equally well characterized as an attempt to prevent failure.
For example, a ritual performed by an athlete before taking a penalty kick may be driven either by the hope of scoring or by the fear of missing.
Second, a crucial aspect unique to harm-prevention rituals is their potential stability over time when the environment is objectively safe.
When a ritual is intended to prevent dire harm (e.g., a plane crash), the rarity of the catastrophe provides repeated apparent confirmation that the ritual has "worked."

In contrast, when a ritual is intended to produce a positive outcome, the frequent failure of that outcome to occur provides more direct evidence contradicting the ritual's effectiveness, which would reduce the value assigned to the preceding action.
Rituals aimed at producing positive outcomes may therefore be less stable, with individuals more likely to abandon or replace an action after an unsuccessful outcome.

Evidence supporting this explanation comes from sports, where superstitious rituals that developed after apparent action-success pairings were reported to be abandoned when they were no longer followed by successful outcomes (Morris et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Evidence supporting this explanation comes from sports, where superstitious rituals that developed after apparent action-success pairings were reported to be abandoned when they were no longer followed by successful outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Morris et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This prediction was not tested in the present model and provides an interesting direction for future work examining whether rituals aimed at producing positive outcomes and rituals aimed at preventing harm differ in how they are acquired, maintained, and replaced.
An unresolved question concerns how the learned action values represented in our model relate to explicit beliefs about the causal efficacy of a ritual.

OCD is often characterized as an ego-dystonic disorder, yet insight varies considerably, with some individuals recognizing that their rituals are unlikely to influence the feared outcome and others experiencing them as more ego-syntonic and believing that their behavior truly affects the outcome (Jalal et al., 2023).

text.text: Our model is limited in its ability to represent this level of conscious causal belief.
We can speculate, however, that automatically acquired action values interact with, and potentially conflict with, a more explicit cognitive map of the environment.

That ishttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?T5IsOU humans may represent a cognitive map of the causal structure of the environment (Moran et al., 2021) , while at the same time acquiring outcome-irrelevant action values despite explicit knowledge that those actions do not predict outcomes (Ben-Artzi, Pereg, et al., 2026).

text.text: Such competing sources of information may offer one way of thinking about the pronounced experience of doubt in OCD.

An automatically learned action value may provide an implicit signal that the ritual "works," which conflicts with an explicit cognitive representation of the environment that suggests that it should not.
Resolving this conflict may be particularly difficult because causal inference about the absence of an effect requires counterfactual reasoning.
After performing the ritual and observing that the feared event did not occur, the individual can only imagine what would have happened had the ritual not been performed.

Counterfactual comparisons are thought to play a central role in causal judgment (Byrnehttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ZedJlq 2016; Gerstenberg, 2024) , while doubt, reduced confidence, and difficulty reaching subjective certainty are prominent features of OCD (Dar et al., 2021; Marton et al., 2019; Samuels et al., 2017).

text.text: Thus, the balance in guiding behavior between automatic credit assignment and an explicit cognitive model of the environment may vary across individuals and circumstances, potentially shaping both the tendency to engage in ritualistic behavior and the degree of causal belief, doubt, and insight associated with it.
This dimension of causal belief was not accounted for in the present simulations and remains an important realm for future work.
Several limitations of the current study should be noted.
First, the present work uses an artificial RL agent and therefore does not provide evidence that the same mechanism operates in human compulsive behavior.
The simulations shown in the manuscript are intended to be a mechanistic illustration of the theoretical account, rather than as a model that should be fitted to clinical data.
Second, the model necessarily simplifies the psychological structure of compulsive rituals.

Internal states are reduced to a binary distinction between anxious and calm states, and agents select among a small number of discrete actions, whereas human threat processing is multidimensional and rituals are often hierarchical, temporally extended, symbolically meaningful, and shaped by verbal rules.

Accordingly, the model should be viewed as a simplified computational account of one potential learning mechanism rather than as an attempt to capture the full complexity of human compulsive behavior.
Finally, the model treats rituals as temporally distinct events to which subsequent outcomes can be assigned.
In everyday life, however, threat expectations are often continuous and temporally diffuse rather than tied to a clearly defined moment.
In particular, the nonoccurrence of a disaster has no physical presence and does not occur at a single identifiable point in time (Balsam & Gallistel, 2009; Gallistel, 2025).
text.formatted: In particular, the nonoccurrence of a disaster has no physical presence and does not occur at a single identifiable point in time <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Balsam & Gallistel, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Gallistel, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that the structured and well-defined nature of rituals may itself create such a temporal anchor, allowing the subsequent occurrence or nonoccurrence of harm to be attributed to the ritual (Hobson et al., 2018; Kurby & Zacks, 2008).

text.text: This assumption, however, was not directly examined in the present model.

Bearing all this in mind, the model should be interpreted as identifying candidate computational principles that may contribute to ritual acquisition and maintenance, rather than as providing a complete account of OCD.

In conclusion, the present model proposes a learning mechanism that may help explain a central puzzle of compulsive ritualistic behavior: how an objectively ineffective action can acquire value as a means of preventing harm (Salkovskis, 1985).

text.text: By formalizing this process, the model complements habitual, anxiety-reducing, and superstitious-learning accounts by specifying how relief and repetition may become attached to one particular action.

Thus, ritualistic behavior may emerge not simply from irrational repetition, but from ordinary reinforcement learning processes that mistakenly assign credit for safety to actions performed under threat.
